library(knitr)

# What this covers

Volunteers have now completed three field seasons of tree inventory (2022, 2025, and 2026 in
progress) and three years of oak seedling inventory (2023-2025) in the East Woods. This report
summarizes what those data say about four questions:

1. How much basal area does each plot carry?
2. What proportion of each plot is oak?
3. How is oak vigor distributed across space, and has it changed since the 2018 IES survey?
4. How many oak seedlings are there, and how has the oak share of regeneration changed?

All numbers come from the scripts in `scripts/`, run in order. Every correction made to the raw
spreadsheets is logged in `data/processed/qaqc_flags.csv` and summarized in the appendix.

<div class="callout">
**Three findings worth knowing before reading any figure.**

1. **The oak share of a plot roughly doubles depending on how you measure it.**
   Oak is `r pct(g("Oak share of live basal area"))` of basal area but only
   `r pct(g("Oak share of live stems"))` of stems, because the oaks are the big trees and
   everything else fills the small size classes.

2. **The apparent improvement in oak vigor since 2018 cannot be separated from a change in
   observers.** Crews differ severalfold in how often they rate an oak as reduced vigor, and the
   crew that rates most stringently shows no significant change. Treat the 2018 comparison as
   inconclusive.

3. **Oak seedlings rose sharply after 2023**, and the rise holds on the plots that genuinely
   repeat -- but the survey moved two months earlier in the season between 2023 and 2024, which
   could produce part of the same pattern.
</div>

# Survey design and what it does and does not support

```{r design}
d1 <- data.frame(
  Dataset = c("Tree survey", "Oak seedling inventory"),
  Years = c("2022, 2025, 2026", "2023, 2024, 2025"),
  Plots = c(paste(nrow(ps), "plot-years"), paste(sum(seedyr$plots), "plot-years")),
  `Plots repeated` = c("none (by design: 5-year rotation)",
                       "29 plots 2023-24, 12 plots 2023-25, none 2024-25"),
  check.names = FALSE)
kable(d1, caption = "Both datasets are rotating panels: a different set of plots each year.")
```

Plots are 0.025 ha (8.92 m radius) with a 10 cm DBH cutoff. Basal area is
`sum(pi * (DBH/2)^2) / 0.025`, expressed in m<sup>2</sup> ha<sup>-1</sup>.

<div class="warn">
**The rotating design means year is confounded with location.** Because a different part of the
woods is visited each year, a raw year-to-year difference mixes real change with the difference
between the plots visited. Wherever this report compares years, it also reports the comparison
restricted to plots that genuinely repeat, and says which one to trust.

Note also that the previous QA/QC script computed basal area as `DBH^2 * 0.005454`, the imperial
ft<sup>2</sup>/acre constant applied to centimeters. Relative comparisons from it were fine, but the
absolute numbers were not m<sup>2</sup> ha<sup>-1</sup>. The values in this report use the metric form.
</div>

# 1. Basal area

```{r ba-stats}
show <- c("Live basal area", "Snag basal area", "Total basal area (live + snag)",
          "Live stem density", "Snag density", "Quadratic mean diameter", "Largest live stem",
          "Species richness")
t1 <- stats[stats$metric %in% show, c("metric", "unit", "n", "mean", "sd", "median", "q25", "q75", "min", "max")]
t1[, 4:10] <- round(t1[, 4:10], 1)
kable(t1, row.names = FALSE, caption = "Plot-level structure. n is plot-years.")
```

Mean live basal area is **`r round(g("Live basal area"), 1)` m<sup>2</sup> ha<sup>-1</sup>**
(median `r round(g("Live basal area", "median"), 1)`), which is what a mature, closed
oak-maple forest should carry. The spread is wide -- the interquartile range alone runs
`r round(g("Live basal area", "q25"), 1)` to `r round(g("Live basal area", "q75"), 1)` -- and one
plot (E-109) was surveyed with no trees at all above the cutoff, which is recorded as a true zero
rather than as missing data.

Standing dead wood is a minor component: snags are `r pct(g("Snag share of total basal area"), 1)`
of total basal area on average and absent entirely from most plots.

```{r fig01, fig.cap="Distribution of live basal area across plots."}
fig.out("fig01_basalarea_distribution")
```

```{r fig02, fig.cap="Live basal area in space."}
fig.out("fig02_basalarea_map")
```

```{r fig03, fig.cap="Live basal area by management unit."}
fig.out("fig03_basalarea_by_unit")
```

The between-unit differences are real but modest next to the plot-to-plot spread within units, and
several units rest on only 2-5 plots. Read the unit ranking as provisional.

# 2. Oak share of each plot

```{r oak-stats}
# The two landscape rows are single pooled values with no distribution, so they get their own table
# rather than six empty columns in the per-plot one.
is.land <- grepl("landscape", stats$metric)
t2 <- stats[grepl("^Oak share", stats$metric) & !is.land,
            c("metric", "n", "mean", "sd", "median", "q25", "q75", "min", "max")]
t2[, 3:9] <- round(t2[, 3:9], 3)
kable(t2, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Oak share per plot, averaged across plots. n is plot-years with any live tree.")

t2b <- stats[is.land, c("metric", "n", "mean")]
t2b$mean <- round(t2b$mean, 3)
names(t2b) <- c("metric", "plot-years", "value")
kable(t2b, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Oak share pooled across the whole sample. This is the share of the forest that is oak, rather than what a typical plot looks like.")
```

This is the number most sensitive to how it is defined:

- **Oak share of basal area**, averaged over plots: `r pct(g("Oak share of live basal area"))`
- **Oak share of stems**, averaged over plots: `r pct(g("Oak share of live stems"))`
- **Oak share of basal area across the whole sample** (basal-area weighted):
  `r pct(g("Oak share of live basal area (landscape, BA-weighted)"))`

The gap between the first two is the substantive result: oak dominates the canopy without dominating
the stem count. The gap between the first and third says the same thing at landscape scale -- plots
with a lot of basal area tend to be the oak-rich ones, so weighting by basal area raises the oak share.

```{r fig06, fig.cap="Oak share by basal area and by stem count, same plots."}
fig.out("fig06_oak_share_distribution")
```

```{r fig05, fig.cap="Size distribution of oak versus everything else."}
fig.out("fig05_dbh_distribution")
```

```{r fig08, fig.cap="Oak share of basal area against oak share of stems, per plot."}
fig.out("fig08_oak_ba_vs_stems")
```

```{r fig07, fig.cap="Oak share of basal area in space."}
fig.out("fig07_oak_share_map")
```

```{r fig04, fig.cap="Species composition of basal area by management unit."}
fig.out("fig04_species_composition")
```

```{r spp-table}
t3 <- head(spp[, c("SppCode", "SppName", "IsOak", "n_stems", "pct_stems", "BA_m2ha", "pct_BA", "n_plots", "DBH_mean")], 12)
t3$BA_m2ha <- round(t3$BA_m2ha, 2)
kable(t3, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Twelve most abundant species by basal area, live stems, all years pooled. BA_m2ha is per hectare of total area sampled.")
```

Note that `ACSA` pools *Acer saccharum* and *A. saccharinum*: the volunteer 4-letter code cannot
separate them, and the 2018 data show both present (703 and 18 stems respectively). Sugar maple is
almost certainly the bulk of it, but the code cannot prove that.

```{r unit-table}
kable(by.unit, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Basal area and oak share by management unit, ordered by oak share of basal area.")
```

# 3. Oak vigor

Vigor is rated 1-3 on live trees only (1 = under 5% dieback; 3 = fewer than 20% of leaves
undamaged). Snags carry no vigor rating and are excluded throughout; 18 snags had been given a
rating of 3, which would have biased the distribution had they been left in.

```{r vigor-summary}
nv <- g("Oak stems with vigor >= 2", "n")
t4 <- stats[grepl("vigor", stats$metric), c("metric", "n", "mean", "sd", "median", "min", "max")]
t4[, 3:7] <- round(t4[, 3:7], 3)
kable(t4, row.names = FALSE, caption = "Oak vigor, summarized across plots with at least one rated oak.")
```

Across `r sum(ps$n_oak_vigor)` rated live oak stems, mean vigor is
`r round(g("Mean oak vigor (1 best - 3 worst)"), 2)` and
`r pct(g("Oak stems with vigor >= 2"), 1)` of stems are rated 2 or 3. **Most oaks in the East Woods
are in the healthiest vigor class.**

## Across space

```{r fig09, fig.cap="Vigor class composition by management unit."}
fig.out("fig09_vigor_by_unit")
```

```{r fig10, fig.cap="Proportion of oaks rated reduced vigor, in space."}
fig.out("fig10_vigor_map")
```

```{r fig11, fig.cap="Reduced vigor against stem size."}
fig.out("fig11_vigor_by_dbh")
```

A mixed model of P(vigor >= 2) with plot and monitoring unit as random effects and crew and DBH as
fixed effects puts the **between-unit variance at exactly zero**. Once plot-to-plot variation and
the difference between crews are accounted for, there is no detectable between-unit signal left.
The unit ranking in the figure above is not distinguishable from noise. Stem size is likewise not a
significant predictor (p = `r signif(mods$p_value[mods$term == "scale(DBH)" & grepl("space", mods$model)][1], 2)`).

## The observer problem

<div class="warn">
**Crew lead is confounded with survey year.** JG and TO surveyed only 2022; GA surveyed 2025 and
2026. No crew spans the 2022/2025 boundary, so for that contrast "year effect" and "observer
effect" are the same thing and no model can separate them.
</div>

```{r crew-table}
# "^crew [A-Z]" and not just "^crew ": the latter also caught the chi-squared row, whose estimate is
# empty by design, putting a stray NA in the table.
ct <- mods[grepl("^crew [A-Z]", mods$term) & mods$model == "Observer effect",
           c("term", "estimate", "note")]
ct$estimate <- round(ct$estimate, 3)
names(ct) <- c("Crew (year)", "Proportion rated vigor >= 2", "Detail")
kable(ct, row.names = FALSE, caption = "How often each crew rated an oak as reduced vigor.")
```

```{r fig12, fig.cap="Between-crew differences in vigor rating."}
fig.out("fig12_observer_effect")
```

## Change since 2018

The 2018 IES survey used the same 1-3 vigor scale, so it provides the baseline. `r nrow(paired)`
plots have rated oaks in both eras. Because 2018 recorded no tree tags, this compares each plot's
oak *population* between eras rather than tracking the same individual stems.

```{r era-table}
et <- data.frame(
  Measure = c("Mean oak vigor (1-3)", "Share of oaks rated vigor 2 or 3"),
  `2018` = c(round(mean(paired$vigor_2018), 3), pct(mean(paired$poor_2018), 1)),
  Resurvey = c(round(mean(paired$vigor_now), 3), pct(mean(paired$poor_now), 1)),
  Change = c(round(mean(paired$d_vigor), 3), paste0(round(100 * mean(paired$d_poor), 1), " pts")),
  `Paired Wilcoxon p` = signif(mods$p_value[mods$model == "2018 vs resurvey (paired Wilcoxon)"], 3),
  check.names = FALSE)
kable(et, row.names = FALSE, caption = paste0("2018 versus resurvey on the ", nrow(paired), " paired plots."))
```

Taken at face value, oak vigor improved: the share of oaks rated 2 or 3 fell from
`r pct(mean(paired$poor_2018), 1)` to `r pct(mean(paired$poor_now), 1)`, and both the paired
Wilcoxon tests and a stem-level mixed model agree (p < 0.01).

```{r fig13a, fig.cap="2018 versus resurvey, by management unit."}
fig.out("fig13a_vigor_2018_dumbbell")
```

```{r fig13b, fig.cap="Per-plot change from 2018 to resurvey."}
fig.out("fig13b_vigor_change_map")
```

**But splitting the same comparison by which crew did the resurvey undoes it.**

```{r crew-era-table}
ce <- mods[mods$model == "2018 vs resurvey, by resurvey crew", c("term", "estimate", "p_value", "note")]
ce$estimate <- paste0(round(100 * ce$estimate, 1), " pts")
ce$p_value <- signif(ce$p_value, 3)
names(ce) <- c("Resurvey crew", "Change in share rated 2-3", "p", "Detail")
kable(ce, row.names = FALSE, caption = "The same 2018-to-now comparison, split by resurvey crew.")
```

```{r fig13c, fig.cap="The 2018-to-now change, split by resurvey crew."}
fig.out("fig13c_vigor_change_by_crew")
```

Nearly all the apparent improvement comes from the 2022 crews, who rated under 2% of oaks as
reduced vigor -- an implausibly low rate. The crew rating most stringently (GA, 69 of the 104 paired
plots) shows a change of only -7 points that is not statistically significant.

<div class="warn">
**Conclusion on vigor through time: inconclusive.** The between-crew spread is as large as the
2018-to-now difference, and the signal disappears in the subset with the most consistent observer.
This is a measurement problem, not a small-sample problem, and more plots will not fix it. See the
recommendations below.
</div>

# 4. Oak seedlings and saplings

```{r seed-table}
st <- seedyr[, c("Year", "plots", "oak_c1_total", "all_c1_total", "oak_per_plot",
                 "prop_oak_pooled", "pct_plots_with_oak")]
st$oak_per_plot <- round(st$oak_per_plot, 2)
st$prop_oak_pooled <- pct(st$prop_oak_pooled, 1)
st$pct_plots_with_oak <- pct(st$pct_plots_with_oak, 1)
names(st) <- c("Year", "Plots", "Oak seedlings", "All seedlings", "Oak per plot",
               "Oak share", "Plots with any oak")
kable(st, row.names = FALSE, caption = "Class 1 seedlings (<1.37 m), the only size class recorded consistently in all three years.")
```

Oak seedling numbers rose sharply: **`r seedyr$oak_c1_total[1]` in 2023, `r seedyr$oak_c1_total[2]`
in 2024, `r seedyr$oak_c1_total[3]` in 2025**, and the oak share of the seedling layer went from
`r pct(seedyr$prop_oak_pooled[1], 1)` to about `r pct(seedyr$prop_oak_pooled[3], 0)`. The share of
plots holding at least one oak seedling also rose steadily, from
`r pct(seedyr$pct_plots_with_oak[1], 1)` to `r pct(seedyr$pct_plots_with_oak[3], 1)`.

```{r fig14, fig.cap="Oak seedling abundance by year."}
fig.out("fig14_oak_seedling_abundance")
```

```{r fig15, fig.cap="Oak share of the Class 1 seedling layer."}
fig.out("fig15_oak_seedling_share")
```

Two things make the *share* move more than oak alone does. Sugar maple collapsed from 988 seedlings
in 2023 to 324 in 2024, and the total count fell from 1,280 to 340 over the three years. So the
rising oak share reflects both more oak and much less of everything else.

```{r fig16, fig.cap="Composition of the seedling layer."}
fig.out("fig16_seedling_composition")
```

## Does the increase survive the design problem?

```{r seed-paired}
sp <- spaired
sp$oak_from <- round(sp$oak_from, 2); sp$oak_to <- round(sp$oak_to, 2)
sp$occ_from <- pct(sp$occ_from, 1); sp$occ_to <- pct(sp$occ_to, 1)
sp$p <- signif(sp$p, 3)
names(sp) <- c("From", "To", "Shared plots", "Oak per plot (from)", "Oak per plot (to)",
               "Plots with oak (from)", "Plots with oak (to)", "Paired Wilcoxon p")
kable(sp, row.names = FALSE, caption = "Restricted to plots surveyed in both years of each pair.")
```

Yes, partly. On the 29 plots surveyed in both 2023 and 2024, mean oak seedlings per plot went from
`r round(spaired$oak_from[spaired$from == 2023 & spaired$to == 2024], 2)` to
`r round(spaired$oak_to[spaired$from == 2023 & spaired$to == 2024], 2)`
(p = `r signif(spaired$p[spaired$from == 2023 & spaired$to == 2024], 2)`). The 2023-2025 pair points
the same way but has only 12 plots and is not significant. 2024 and 2025 share no plots at all, so
that step cannot be checked.

A negative binomial model of oak counts with monitoring unit held constant gives the same answer
(2024 vs 2023: p = `r signif(smods$p_value[smods$term == "YearF2024"][1], 2)`), as does the
occupancy test (p = `r signif(smods$p_value[grepl("occupancy", smods$model)][1], 3)`), which is
insensitive to a few plots carrying very large counts.

```{r fig17, fig.cap="Paired-plot change in oak seedlings."}
fig.out("fig17_seedling_paired_change")
```

```{r fig18, fig.cap="Oak seedlings by year and location."}
fig.out("fig18_oak_seedling_map")
```

<div class="warn">
**Two caveats on the seedling trend.**

1. **Season.** 2023 was surveyed late September to October, 2024 in July and August. First-year oak
seedlings emerge in spring and can be browsed or drop leaves by autumn, so a late survey may simply
count fewer of them. This alone could produce part of the 2023-to-2024 jump.

2. **Size classes.** Only 26 of 183 species records in 2023 have any Class 2 or 3 entry, against
near-complete recording in 2024 and 2025. Either the larger classes were not recorded in 2023 or the
sapling layer genuinely changed. **This needs confirming before Class 2-3 numbers are compared
across years**; everything above deliberately uses Class 1 only.
</div>

Also worth flagging for management: invasive shrubs (*Lonicera*, *Rhamnus*, *Rosa multiflora*,
*Euonymus*) were 5%, 10%, and 2% of Class 1 seedlings across the three years -- a smaller share than
oak in 2024-25, but a persistent presence in the regeneration layer.

# What we can and cannot say

```{r verdicts}
v <- data.frame(
  Question = c("Basal area per plot",
               "Oak proportion per plot",
               "Oak vigor across space",
               "Oak vigor through time",
               "Oak seedling abundance",
               "Oak share of seedlings"),
  Answer = c(paste0("Mean ", round(g("Live basal area"), 1), " m2/ha (median ",
                    round(g("Live basal area", "median"), 1), "), range 0-",
                    round(g("Live basal area", "max"), 0)),
             paste0(pct(g("Oak share of live basal area")), " of basal area but only ",
                    pct(g("Oak share of live stems")), " of stems"),
             paste0(pct(g("Oak stems with vigor >= 2"), 1), " of oaks rated 2 or 3; ",
                    "no detectable difference between units"),
             "Apparent improvement, but not separable from a change in observers",
             paste0("Rose from ", seedyr$oak_c1_total[1], " to ", seedyr$oak_c1_total[2],
                    " to ", seedyr$oak_c1_total[3], "; holds on repeated plots"),
             paste0("Rose from ", pct(seedyr$prop_oak_pooled[1], 1), " to ",
                    pct(seedyr$prop_oak_pooled[3], 0), " of Class 1 seedlings")),
  Confidence = c("High", "High", "Moderate", "**Inconclusive**", "Moderate", "Moderate"))
kable(v, row.names = FALSE)
```

## Decisions we need from the field team

1. **Plot A-133 versus AZ-133.** A-133 has stems recorded in both 2022 and 2025, which the rotating
   design should not allow. The Plot List note on AZ-133 reads *"stake says A-133; might've done
   wrong plot."* One of those two visits probably surveyed a different plot. Both are currently
   retained and flagged.
2. **Plot KK-116, 2026.** All 29 stems have canopy-position codes (I, S) in the Vigor Rating column.
   Vigor is currently set to missing for that plot; the ratings may be recoverable from the paper
   sheets.
3. **2023 Class 2 and 3 seedlings.** Were the larger size classes actually recorded that year?
4. **Species codes PESE and CESA** (1 stem each) are not recognized. PESE may be a typo for PRSE.

## Recommendations for the protocol

1. **Calibrate vigor rating across crews.** This is the highest-value change available. A short
   annual calibration -- all crew leads rate the same 15-20 trees and compare -- would make vigor
   comparable between years and would make the 2018 comparison interpretable. As it stands, vigor is
   the one measure in this dataset that cannot be compared across time.
2. **Record a search area for the seedling layer.** The protocol does not state one, so seedling
   counts cannot be converted to densities per hectare or compared with other studies.
3. **Fix the survey window.** Sampling seedlings in July one year and October the next makes real
   change hard to distinguish from phenology. Pick a window and hold it.
4. **Keep some plots in every year's rotation.** A small permanent panel (even 10-15 plots visited
   annually) would give a within-plot time series and resolve exactly the ambiguities that limit
   this report.
5. **Add sheet validation.** Dropdown lists for species code, canopy position, and vigor would
   prevent most of the errors in the appendix, including the column-shift at KK-116.

# Appendix: data quality

`r nrow(flags)` items were flagged during cleaning. Nothing was silently dropped; the full log with
plot and tag numbers is in `data/processed/qaqc_flags.csv`.

```{r flag-table}
ft <- as.data.frame(table(Dataset = flags$dataset, Issue = flags$issue))
ft <- ft[ft$Freq > 0, ]
act <- tapply(flags$action, paste(flags$dataset, flags$issue), function(x) paste(unique(x), collapse = "; "))
ft$Action <- act[paste(ft$Dataset, ft$Issue)]
ft <- ft[order(ft$Dataset, -ft$Freq), c("Dataset", "Issue", "Freq", "Action")]
names(ft)[3] <- "Records"
kable(ft, row.names = FALSE, caption = "Every issue found and what was done about it.")
```

```{r counts}
cnt <- data.frame(
  Step = c("Tree survey rows in the sheet", "Rows with a survey date",
           "Analysis-ready stems", "Plots surveyed", "Plots excluded (could not be located)",
           "Seedling rows in the three tabs", "Analysis-ready seedling records",
           "Seedling plot-years"),
  Count = c(1389, 1332, sum(ps$stems_live + ps$stems_snag), nrow(ps), 2,
            1065, nrow(rd("seedlings_clean.csv")), sum(seedyr$plots)))
kable(cnt, row.names = FALSE, caption = "Row counts from raw sheet to analysis.")
```

## Model output

```{r model-table}
mm <- rbind(mods, smods)
mm$estimate <- signif(mm$estimate, 4)
mm$se <- signif(mm$se, 3); mm$statistic <- signif(mm$statistic, 3); mm$p_value <- signif(mm$p_value, 3)
# Descriptive rows have no standard error or p-value; an empty cell reads better than "NA"
for (cc in c("estimate", "se", "statistic", "p_value")) {
  mm[[cc]] <- ifelse(is.na(mm[[cc]]), "", format(mm[[cc]], trim = TRUE))
}
kable(mm, row.names = FALSE, caption = "All fitted models and tests. Also in data/processed/model_summaries*.csv.")
```

## Reproducing this report

```
Rscript scripts/0_data_download.R      # pull and cache both Google Sheets
Rscript scripts/1_qaqc_clean.R         # clean, log every correction
Rscript scripts/2_species_crosswalk.R  # link 2018 six-letter codes to volunteer four-letter codes
Rscript scripts/3_plot_summaries.R     # plot-level metrics and summary statistics
Rscript scripts/3b_figures_basalarea.R # figures 1-8
Rscript scripts/4_vigor_analysis.R     # figures 9-13, vigor models
Rscript scripts/5_seedling_analysis.R  # figures 14-18, seedling models
Rscript scripts/7_render_report.R      # knits this report
```

Run from the project root. Script 0 needs a Google account with access to both sheets; everything
after it works offline from the dated snapshots in `data/raw_gsheet/`. Use
`scripts/7_render_report.R` rather than calling `rmarkdown::render` directly -- it sets the working
directory and pandoc path that the relative figure paths depend on.
